title: Change of Measure, Risk-Neutrality and Feynman-Kac
objectives: Explain the Radon-Nikodym density as a re-weighting of scenario probabilities and compute expectations under a changed measure
Derive the risk-neutral probability in a two-state market and show it prices by no-arbitrage, not by expected value under physical probabilities
State Girsanov's theorem and apply it to shift the drift of a geometric Brownian motion from $\mu$ to $r$
State the Feynman-Kac representation connecting SDE expectations to parabolic PDEs
Price a European call with the Black-Scholes formula and link each formula input to the underlying PDE/expectation machinery
motivation: You cannot price a derivative by taking an expectation under real-world probabilities: investors demand a risk premium, and two traders with different risk appetites would get different prices. Arbitrage-free pricing fixes this by changing the measure - re-weighting scenarios so that every traded asset, discounted, is a martingale. This lesson makes 'change of measure' concrete, states the two theorems that carry the whole edifice (Girsanov and Feynman-Kac), and lands on Black-Scholes as the canonical application.

blocks.md: A stochastic process - say the path of a stock price - is a set of possible outcomes. A **probability measure** decides how much weight each outcome gets. The same collection of paths can carry different measures: the **physical (real-world) measure** $\mathbb{P}$ describes what you *expect* to happen, estimated from data; an equivalent **pricing measure** $\mathbb{Q}$ describes the weights under which the market is arbitrage-free. 'Equivalent' means $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ agree on which paths are possible - they only redistribute the weights, never move probability from a possible path to an impossible one.

Changing between equivalent measures is done multiplicatively, by a **Radon-Nikodym density** $Z = d\mathbb{Q}/d\mathbb{P}$: a positive random variable with $\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[Z] = 1$. Each $\mathbb{P}$-scenario of probability $p$ is re-weighted to $\mathbb{Q}$-probability $p \cdot Z$. Expectations transform by $\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[X] = \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[Z X]$ - the density is a likelihood-ratio applied payoff-wise.

blocks.title: Worked example: re-weighting a two-state world
items: Target measure $\mathbb{Q}$: both states equally likely ($0.5$, $0.5$).
Check normalisation: $\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[Z] = 0.6 \times 0.8333 + 0.4 \times 1.25 = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1$. A density that failed this check would not be a measure.

blocks.text: Why the risk-neutral measure matters for pricing

blocks.md: Set up a market: stock today $S_0 = 100$; in one period it moves to $S_u = 110$ or $S_d = 90$; the interest rate is zero. A call struck at $K = 100$ pays $10$ in the up state and $0$ in the down state. Under the physical measure with $p = 0.6$, the expected payoff is $0.6 \times 10 = 6$ - but discounting that at the risk-free rate and calling it a price invites arbitrage, because $p = 0.6$ embeds a risk premium, not a hedging argument.

The fix is to find $q$ such that the *expected* stock return under those weights equals the risk-free rate: $q \times 110 + (1-q) \times 90 = 100$, so $90 + 20q = 100$ and $q = 0.5$. These $\mathbb{Q}$-weights are called **risk-neutral** because under them every asset earns exactly the risk-free rate - investors behave as if indifferent to risk. The price is then the discounted $\mathbb{Q}$-expectation of the payoff: $0.5 \times 10 + 0.5 \times 0 = \$5$.

blocks.title: No-arbitrage, not wishful thinking
blocks.md: Replication confirms \$5: hold $\Delta = (10-0)/(110-90) = 0.5$ shares and borrow $0.5 \times 110 - 10 = \$. Cost today: $0.5 \times 100 - 45 = \$, and it reproduces the call payoff in both states. Any other price is free money. The Fundamental Theorems of Asset Pricing make this precise: no arbitrage is equivalent to the existence of an equivalent martingale measure, and completeness makes it unique.

In continuous time the density becomes a stochastic process. Given a Brownian motion $W^{\mathbb{P}}$ under $\mathbb{P}$ and a suitable adapted process $\theta_t$, define $Z_t = \exp\big(-\int_0^t \theta_s \, dW^{\mathbb{P}}_s - \tfrac{1}{2}\int_0^t \theta_s^2 \, ds\big)$. When $\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[Z_T] = 1$, $Z$ defines an equivalent measure $\mathbb{Q}$ via $d\mathbb{Q} = Z_T \, d\mathbb{P}$, and $W^{\mathbb{Q}}_t = W^{\mathbb{P}}_t + \int_0^t \theta_s \, ds$ is a Brownian motion **under $\mathbb{Q}$**. Intuitively, the density re-weights paths so that a *different* shifted process looks like pure noise. A full proof needs Novikov's condition and martingale representation; here we only need the consequence.
The consequence is a one-line drift transplant. Writing $dW^{\mathbb{P}} = dW^{\mathbb{Q}} - \theta \, dt$, the stock dynamics $dS/S = \mu \, dt + \sigma \, dW^{\mathbb{P}}$ become

blocks.tex: dS = \sigma S\, dW^{\mathbb{Q}} + (\mu - \sigma\theta)\, S\, dt \;\xrightarrow[\theta = (\mu - r)/\sigma]{}\; dS = r\,S\,dt + \sigma\,S\,dW^{\mathbb{Q}}
blocks.caption: Girsanov shifts the drift by $-\sigma\theta$; choosing the market price of risk $\theta = (\mu-r)/\sigma$ leaves exactly the risk-free drift $r$.

blocks.title: What changes and what cannot
blocks.md: A change of measure moves the **drift** of an Itô process; the **diffusion (volatility) coefficient is untouched**, because Girsanov only tilts probabilities, not the quadratic variation of the paths. That is why $\sigma$ appears identically under $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ - and why implied volatility is a property of the market's pricing measure, not of the stock's real-world dynamics.

blocks.text: Feynman-Kac: from expectations to PDEs and back

blocks.md: Feynman-Kac is the bridge between the two languages of quant finance. Stated for a diffusion $dX = a(X)\,dt + b(X)\,dW^{\mathbb{Q}}$ and a terminal payoff $g$: the function $V(t,x) = \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}\big[e^{-r(T-t)} g(X_T) \,\big|\, X_t = x\big]$ satisfies the parabolic PDE

blocks.tex: \frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + a(x)\,\frac{\partial V}{\partial x} + \tfrac{1}{2}\,b^2(x)\,\frac{\partial^2 V}{\partial x^2} - r\,V = 0, \qquad V(T,x) = g(x)
blocks.caption: The drift enters as first-order transport, the (squared) diffusion as second-order spreading, and discounting as the sink term $-rV$.

blocks.md: Read it in both directions. SDE $\to$ PDE: an expectation you cannot compute analytically becomes a PDE you can solve numerically. PDE $\to$ SDE: a pricing PDE's solution has a probabilistic representation, so Monte Carlo simulation is a legitimate solver. The proof combines Itô's lemma (from the previous lesson) applied to $e^{-r(T-t)}g(X_T)$ with the martingale property under $\mathbb{Q}$.

Run the pipeline end to end. Under $\mathbb{Q}$, $dS = rS\,dt + \sigma S\,dW^{\mathbb{Q}}$, so $a(S) = rS$ and $b(S) = \sigma S$. Feynman-Kac turns the price of a European call into the PDE $V_t + rS V_S + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 V_{SS} - rV = 0$ with terminal condition $V(T,S) = (S-K)^+$. Solving it (or directly computing the lognormal expectation) yields

blocks.tex: C = S_0\,N(d_1) - K e^{-rT} N(d_2), \qquad d_1 = \frac{\ln(S_0/K) + (r + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}, \quad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T}
blocks.caption: $N$ is the standard normal CDF. Notice $\mu$ is nowhere: the real-world drift has been priced away by the measure change.

blocks.title: Worked example: one-year ATM call
items: $C \approx \$10.45$ per share on a notional of \$100 - the whole Girsanov/Feynman-Kac pipeline compressed into one number.

blocks.code:
import math

def ncdf(x):
    return 0.5 * (1.0 + math.erf(x / math.sqrt(2.0)))

S0, K, sigma, r, T = 100.0, 100.0, 0.20, 0.05, 1.0
d1 = (math.log(S0 / K) + (r + 0.5 * sigma ** 2) * T) / (sigma * math.sqrt(T))
d2 = d1 - sigma * math.sqrt(T)
call = S0 * ncdf(d1) - K * math.exp(-r * T) * ncdf(d2)
print(round(call, 2))   # 10.45
blocks.caption: math.erf gives the normal CDF; the code reproduces the hand computation exactly.
Move the inputs and watch $d_1$, $d_2$ and the call price respond. Only $r$ and $\sigma$ survive from the measure change - $\mu$ never appears.

guidedExercise.prompt: In the two-state market of this lesson ($S_0 = 100$, $S_u = 110$, $S_d = 90$, $r = 0$): (a) compute the risk-neutral probability $q$ of the up state; (b) price a **put** struck at $K = 100$ by discounted $\mathbb{Q}$-expectation; (c) verify your price by replication (shares plus borrowing).
hints: Risk-neutral means the expected stock price under $\mathbb{Q}$ equals $S_0 (1+r)$.
The put pays $(K - S_T)^+$: 10 in the down state, 0 in the up state.
Replication: find $\Delta$ with $\Delta \cdot 110 + B = 0$ and $\Delta \cdot 90 + B = 10$.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) $110q + 90(1-q) = 100 \Rightarrow q = 0.5$. (b) Payoff: 10 (down), 0 (up). Price $= e^{-rT}[q \times 0 + (1-q) \times 10] = 0.5 \times 10 = \$. (c) Solve $\Delta \cdot 110 + B = 0$ and $\Delta \cdot 90 + B = 10$: subtract to get $20\Delta = -10$, so $\Delta = -0.5$ shares (short stock), and $B = 55$ invested at the risk-free rate. Cost today $= -0.5 \times 100 + 55 = \$. Both methods agree - the measure change did the hedging arithmetic for us.

independentExercise.prompt: A stock trades at $S_0 = 200$ and under $\mathbb{P}$ has $\mu = 0.12$, $\sigma = 0.30$. The risk-free rate is $r = 0.03$. (a) Compute the market price of risk $\theta$. (b) Write the stock's SDE under $\mathbb{Q}$. (c) Using the $\mathbb{Q}$-dynamics, price a one-year European digital call paying $1{,}000 if $S_T \ge 200$ (assume $\mathbb{Q}$-probability $S_T \ge 200$ is 0.560) by discounted expectation. (d) Would this price change if $\mu$ were 0.20 instead? Explain why.
hints: Under $\mathbb{Q}$ the drift is $r$, volatility unchanged.
Discount at $e^{-rT}$; then ask which inputs of $\theta$ depend on $\mu$.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $\theta = (0.12 - 0.03)/0.30 = 0.09/0.30 = 0.30$. (b) $dS = 0.03\,S\,dt + 0.30\,S\,dW^{\mathbb{Q}}$. (c) Price $= e^{-0.03 \times 1} \times 1000 \times 0.560 = 970.45 \times 0.560 \approx \$. (d) No: $\mu$ only enters $\theta$, which is exactly the knob Girsanov turns to restore drift $r$. The $\mathbb{Q}$-dynamics - and hence the price - are identical for any $\mu$; the real-world drift affects hedge *quantities* (via delta over time) but not the arbitrage-free price.

commonMistakes: Pricing with physical-measure probabilities: $\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[\text{payoff}]$ embeds a risk premium and is generally not arbitrage-free.
Believing Girsanov changes volatility - only the drift moves; $\sigma$ is measure-invariant.
Forgetting the discount factor $e^{-rT}$ when converting a $\mathbb{Q}$-expectation into a today's price.
Writing $dW^{\mathbb{Q}} = dW^{\mathbb{P}} + \theta\,dt$ with the wrong sign: under $\mathbb{Q}$ the drift must come out as $r$, which pins the sign.
realWorldApplication: Every derivatives desk prices from a calibrated pricing measure: implied volatilities are observations about $\mathbb{Q}$, while historical volatility and drift estimates describe $\mathbb{P}$. Risk systems run the same models under both measures and keep the two strictly separated.
quantFinanceApplication: Black-Scholes is Feynman-Kac applied to risk-neutral geometric Brownian motion; the same pipeline (change measure, take discounted $\mathbb{Q}$-expectation, or solve the resulting PDE) prices exotics, and its Monte-Carlo/PDE duality is why every bank runs both an MC engine and a PDE solver against the same models.
summary: A change of measure re-weights scenario probabilities via a density $Z = d\mathbb{Q}/d\mathbb{P}$ with $\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[Z] = 1$; $\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[X] = \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[ZX]$.
Risk-neutral pricing: choose $\mathbb{Q}$ so discounted assets are martingales; price $= e^{-rT}\,\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\text{payoff}]$. No arbitrage guarantees existence, completeness uniqueness.

Girsanov: $dW^{\mathbb{Q}} = dW^{\mathbb{P}} + \theta\,dt$ shifts drifts by $-\sigma\theta$ and leaves volatility unchanged; $\theta = (\mu - r)/\sigma$ gives $dS = rS\,dt + \sigma S\,dW^{\mathbb{Q}}$.
Feynman-Kac converts discounted $\mathbb{Q}$-expectations into parabolic PDEs (and back): $V_t + aV_x + \tfrac12 b^2 V_{xx} - rV = 0$, $V(T,x) = g(x)$.
Black-Scholes is the canonical application: $C = S_0 N(d_1) - Ke^{-rT}N(d_2)$; for $S_0=K=100$, $\sigma=0.2$, $r=0.05$, $T=1$ the call is worth about \$10.45.

quiz.prompt: Under a change of measure from $\mathbb{P}$ to $\mathbb{Q}$ via Girsanov, which property of an Itô process changes?
options: The quadratic variation of the paths
quiz.explanation: Girsanov tilts probabilities, shifting the drift by $-\sigma\theta$. The volatility, the support of the process (possible paths) and hence quadratic variation are unchanged - equivalence forbids moving weight onto impossible paths.

quiz.prompt: Stock: $S_0 = 100$, moving to $110$ (up) or $90$ (down) in one period, $r = 0$. What is the risk-neutral probability of the up state?
quiz.explanation: Risk-neutrality requires $110q + 90(1-q) = 100$, so $20q = 10$ and $q = 0.5$ - regardless of the physical probability $p$.

quiz.prompt: In the same market, a call struck at $K = 100$ pays 10 if the stock goes up and 0 if it goes down. What is its no-arbitrage price?
quiz.explanation: Discounted $\mathbb{Q}$-expectation: $1 \times (0.5 \times 10 + 0.5 \times 0) = \$5$. Replication ($0.5$ shares, borrow \$45) confirms it; the physical expectation $0.6 \times 10 = 6$ would admit arbitrage.

quiz.prompt: Feynman-Kac lets a desk do which of the following?
options: Convert a discounted expectation under $\mathbb{Q}$ into a PDE, and a PDE back into a Monte Carlo problem
Guarantee the physical drift $\mu$ appears in option prices
Prove that all equivalent measures are identical
quiz.explanation: Feynman-Kac is the SDE $\leftrightarrow$ PDE dictionary: expectations become parabolic PDEs and PDE solutions have probabilistic representations. It says nothing about removing $\sigma$, and $\mu$ is precisely what gets priced out.

quiz.prompt: In one or two sentences: why can't we simply discount $\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[\text{payoff}]$ at the risk-free rate to get an option price?
quiz.modelAnswer: Physical probabilities embed investors' risk preferences, so the discounted physical expectation is generally not arbitrage-free - it ignores the market price of risk and need not match the replicating portfolio's cost. Pricing must use the risk-neutral measure, under which discounted asset prices are martingales.
quiz.explanation: $\mathbb{P}$ weights scenarios by how likely they are; pricing needs weights under which the discounted stock is a martingale. The gap between the two is the risk premium.

flashcards.back: A positive random variable with $\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[Z] = 1$ that re-weights each scenario: $\mathbb{Q}(A) = \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[Z \mathbf{1}_A]$, and $\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[X] = \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[ZX]$.

$dW^{\mathbb{Q}} = dW^{\mathbb{P}} + \theta\,dt$ makes $W^{\mathbb{Q}}$ a $\mathbb{Q}$-Brownian motion; $dS/S = \mu\,dt + \sigma\,dW^{\mathbb{P}}$ becomes $dS/S = (\mu - \sigma\theta)\,dt + \sigma\,dW^{\mathbb{Q}}$. Choose $\theta = (\mu - r)/\sigma$.
$V(t,x) = \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[e^{-r(T-t)}g(X_T)\,|\,X_t=x]$ solves $V_t + a(x)V_x + \tfrac12 b^2(x)V_{xx} - rV = 0$ with $V(T,x) = g(x)$.

flashcards.front: Risk-neutral measure - what is 'neutral' about it?
flashcards.back: Under $\mathbb{Q}$ every (discounted) traded asset is a martingale: all assets earn exactly the risk-free rate, as if investors were indifferent to risk. It prices by arbitrage, not by preferences.
Equivalent measures agree on which paths are possible, so quadratic variation - and hence $\sigma$ - is identical under $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$; only the drift moves.
